name: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
intent: Fetch the few passages that matter from your own documents at question time and put them in the model's prompt, so answers are grounded, current and citable.
scenario: A support bot answers questions from a 7-page help centre. A customer asks how long they have to send back a laptop. The bot must find the one sentence that says 30 days, not the similar-looking shipping, warranty or old 2023 text, and cite it.
problem: A language model only knows its training data: nothing private, nothing after its cutoff, and no way to show where an answer came from. Pasting every document into the prompt does not scale: context is limited, you pay per token, latency grows with prompt length, and accuracy tends to drop when the right passage is buried in noise. Retrieval has to pick a few passages, and picking wrongly produces fluent, confident, cited and wrong answers.

howItWorks.title: Chunk and index offline
howItWorks.text: Documents are split into chunks, typically a few hundred tokens each with 10 to 20 percent overlap, or split along headings and paragraphs. Each chunk is stored with its text, keyword postings, an embedding vector, the source id and its access rules. Chunk size is the main recall versus precision lever: small chunks match precisely but may cut the answer in half, large chunks keep context but dilute the match and cost more tokens.

howItWorks.title: Rewrite the query and retrieve with both keyword and vector search
howItWorks.text: The question may be rewritten (resolve 'it' from chat history, expand abbreviations, split a compound question). Keyword search (BM25) is strong on exact names, codes and numbers; vector search is strong on paraphrase ('send back' versus 'return'). Hybrid retrieval runs both and merges the lists, often with reciprocal rank fusion. Fetch generously, for example 20 to 100 candidates, because the next stage prunes.

howItWorks.title: Rerank the candidates
howItWorks.text: A reranker, usually a cross-encoder that reads the query and one chunk together, scores each candidate more accurately than the index could. It is too slow to run over the whole corpus (tens of milliseconds per batch of candidates on a GPU), which is why the cheap index narrows first and the reranker orders the survivors. Keep the top 3 to 10.

howItWorks.title: Assemble context within a token budget
howItWorks.text: The prompt has a fixed window and every token costs money and latency. Pack the best chunks in rank order until the budget is spent, drop duplicates from overlapping chunks, tag each with a citation id, and keep the instructions and the answer room outside the budget. More context is not better: models use the start and end of a long prompt more reliably than the middle, and irrelevant chunks invite wrong answers.

howItWorks.title: Generate a grounded, cited answer, or decline
howItWorks.text: The instruction tells the model to answer only from the sources, to cite them, and to say so when they do not contain the answer. Check that the cited ids were actually in the prompt. Retrieval confidence (a score threshold, or no chunk passing the reranker) is the cheapest signal for abstaining. Keep the index fresh: re-embed changed pages, delete removed ones, and filter by the caller's permissions before ranking.

pros: Answers use private and recent knowledge without retraining the model
Every claim can point to a source the user can open and check
Updating knowledge is an index write, not a training run
Access control and deletion are enforceable at the document level, which weights cannot offer
cons: Quality is capped by retrieval: if the right chunk is not in the prompt, no model can recover it
Many knobs interact (chunking, k, rerank, budget) and need an evaluation set to tune
Adds latency (embedding the query, search, rerank) and an index to operate and keep fresh
Long prompts raise cost per request and can lower accuracy
whenToUse: Questions over private, large or frequently changing documents
Answers that must cite a source or be auditable
Knowledge that differs per user or tenant and must respect permissions
whenNotToUse: The whole corpus fits comfortably in the prompt and is read rarely: just put it in, with prompt caching
Questions need aggregation or exact lookup over structured data: use SQL or an API call as a tool
You need a new style, format or skill from the model rather than facts: that is fine-tuning territory
You cannot evaluate retrieval separately from generation, since you will not know which half is failing
pitfalls: Chunk boundaries cutting the answer, for example the condition in one chunk and the number in the next, so only half arrives
Retrieving the wrong but similar text: shipping and warranty pages share the vocabulary of a returns question
A stale index: the old policy is still embedded and outranks or sits beside the new one, so the model cites outdated facts
Context stuffing: raising top-k to be safe buries the answer and can reduce accuracy while raising cost
No no-answer path: the model is handed plausible chunks and improvises instead of saying it does not know
Applying access control after retrieval or only in the UI: restricted chunks reach the prompt, and from there the answer
Evaluating only the final answer, so you cannot tell whether retrieval or generation broke; measure recall of the right chunk separately

roles.label: Source documents
roles.description: The pages, tickets or files that hold the truth. They change, and some are restricted.

roles.label: Search index
roles.description: Holds chunks with keyword postings, embedding vectors, source ids and access rules.

roles.label: Application
roles.description: Receives the question, assembles the prompt within the token budget and checks the citations.

roles.label: Retriever and reranker
roles.description: Rewrites the query, fetches candidates by keyword and vector, and reorders them.

roles.label: Language model
roles.description: Writes the answer from the sources in its prompt, or says they are not enough.

quiz.question: A support bot uses keyword search only. A customer asks how long they have to send back a laptop. The policy page says 'return window' and never uses the words 'send back', so the bot retrieves the shipping page instead. What helps most?
options: Add vector search and merge it with keyword results
Raise the number of keyword results from 5 to 50
Switch to a larger generation model
Make every chunk twice as long
quiz.explanation: Vector search matches meaning, so 'send back' finds 'return window', while keyword search stays strong on exact names and codes. Merging both is hybrid retrieval. A bigger keyword list or model cannot use a page that never matched, and longer chunks do not change the vocabulary gap.

quiz.question: The return policy reads 'Laptops can be returned within 30 days' in one chunk and 'only if unopened' at the start of the next. The index uses fixed 200-token windows that cut through that paragraph. The bot says all laptops can be returned. What is the best fix?
options: Use an embedding model with more dimensions
Ask the model to double-check its answer
quiz.explanation: The condition and the number landed in different chunks, so only half the rule reached the prompt. Chunking along natural boundaries with overlap keeps them together. A larger top-k mostly adds noise, and a better embedding or a re-check cannot restore text that was never in the prompt.

quiz.question: An internal assistant answers from HR documents. Staff may only read documents for their own department. Which design keeps restricted text out of answers?
options: Hide the restricted citations in the user interface
Tell the model not to reveal other departments' content
Filter the model's answer for restricted phrases afterwards
Filter by the caller's permissions before ranking chunks
quiz.explanation: Anything that reaches the prompt can leak into the answer, so restricted chunks must never be retrieved for that caller. Filtering at retrieval, before ranking, enforces this at the document level. UI hiding, instructions to the model and output filtering all act after the text is already in the prompt.
